beats.marks: Say nothing here. This is up while you are being introduced and getting settled. Do not talk over your own title card.

visual.title:
None of this
is accounting.

a.lines:
B.S. Biomedical Engineering
B.A. Business Economics

b.lines:
7× Salesforce Certified · AWS CCP
CompTIA A+, Network+, Security+

visual.tail: Let me tell you why it's all the same job.

beats.opener: Before I get into anything, I want to name the obvious thing about my resume.
beats.rest:
I have a degree in biomedical engineering. I have seven Salesforce certifications and I passed the CISSP exam.

None of that is accounting.
beats.marks: PAUSE — two beats. Hands still. Let the objection land before you answer it.

beats.opener: But I also double majored. Business economics, same four years.
beats.rest:
And that major had accounting classes in it, which at nineteen I did not think much about at all.

So the honest version is: I picked both halves of this job when I was nineteen. Engineering, which is how you build the system. And economics, which is what's moving through it. Then I spent about a decade finding out why.

Let me walk you through that decade.

visual.title:
I was the guy
entering the data.
visual.sub: Lab tech. Bench work. Somebody else's software.

beats.opener: My first job out of school was as a lab tech.
beats.rest:
And I'll be honest about that job, because it matters later — it was not the interesting part. I did bench work. Collected samples, ran assays, and typed numbers into somebody else's software.

I was the guy entering the data.

Hold onto that. Almost everything I've done since comes back to it.
beats.marks: Plant. Say "I was the guy entering the data" plainly — no emphasis. It pays off on the CDTFA slide.

visual.title: Then I touched Excel.
visual.sub: Years of historical preclinical data — toxicology and pharmacology.
visual.tail: Data that had a shape — and a shape that was enforced.

beats.opener: Then I got to Amgen, and the actual work turned out to be Excel.
beats.rest:
They had years of historical preclinical data — drug toxicology and pharmacology studies — sitting in spreadsheets. And a spreadsheet will let you type anything into any cell. Nothing enforces that the number in the box is the right kind of number, or that it belongs to the study you think it belongs to.

So I wrote VBA to pull all of it out and move it into a relational database. Where the data had a shape, and the shape was enforced.

beats.opener: That's the first time I understood what I actually liked. It wasn't the science.
beats.rest: It was that the data was in the wrong shape, and somebody had to fix that.
beats.marks: Do NOT say this is what Vast is going through. Let it sit. Cash it in during Topic 2.

visual.title:
Nobody plans to become
a Salesforce admin.
visual.sub: Contract research organization — sample collection and processing. I volunteered once. Six months later I was the department.

beats.opener: Next was a CRO — a contract research organization. We collected and processed samples for other people's studies.
beats.rest:
They ran on Salesforce and they needed somebody to administer it. I raised my hand, mostly out of curiosity.

That's how you become a Salesforce admin, by the way. Nobody applies for it. You volunteer once, and six months later you are the department.
beats.marks: FIRST LAUGH. Say it flat and dry — do not sell it. Then hold. Do not walk on the laugh.

visual.title: I built the system I used to hate using.

items.lead: LIMS — laboratory information management, on Salesforce
items.sub: Sample intake · chain of custody · what has been run on what

items.lead: I'd used the big ones as a tech
items.sub: They're built for the person signing the purchase order — not the person at the bench with a sample in one hand and a barcode gun in the other.

visual.callout: And I could only build it because I'd been the one using it.

beats.opener: The main thing I built there was a LIMS — laboratory information management system.
beats.rest:
Sample intake, chain of custody, where every sample is, what's been run on it.

Here's the part that matters. I had already used LIMS systems — at Amgen, in the lab, as a tech. I knew exactly what they felt like from the entry side. And the big ones are built for the person who signs the purchase order, not for the person standing at the bench with a sample in one hand and a barcode gun in the other.

So I built the simplified version that fit how the work actually happened.

beats.opener: I built the system I used to hate using.
beats.rest: And I could only do that because I had been the one using it.
beats.marks: PAUSE after the first line. This is one of the two lines carrying the whole section.

visual.title:
I keep automating
the job I just did.
visual.tail: Do the job by hand first. Feel where it hurts. Then build the thing that removes it.

beats.opener: If you've been keeping score, there's a pattern here, and I didn't notice it for years.
beats.rest:
I did the bench work, then I built the lab system. I did the data entry, then I built the database.

Every time, the sequence is identical. Do the job by hand first. Feel exactly where it hurts. Then build the thing that takes it away.

I'm going to come back to this at the very end, when I tell you what I'd do in my first ninety days here. Because that plan isn't a theory I came up with for this interview.

It's just the only way I've ever worked.
beats.marks: THROUGH-LINE, pass 1 of 3. Returns at the end of Topic 1, and again at the close.

visual.title: Same move. Bigger.

items.sub: Project management for a live practice
Custom survey platform, written in Apex
Automated AR/AP payment sync

visual.callout: The last one is the one that changed everything.

beats.opener: Then ForensisGroup — an expert witness referral firm that ran its whole practice on Salesforce. Same move, bigger scale.
beats.rest: I built PMify, project management for live cases. Survey Builder, a custom survey platform in Apex. And an automated AR/AP payment sync between Salesforce and QuickBooks.

beats.opener: That last one changed my life and I had no idea at the time.
beats.rest:
Because to build it, I had to learn what actually happens to a payment. Not the button — the entry. What gets debited, what gets credited, when it's recognized, and what breaks downstream in the books if I get any of it wrong.

I was building accounting plumbing.

And somewhere in there I noticed I cared more about what was moving through the pipe than about the pipe.
beats.marks: Slow down on "than about the pipe." That's the turn of the whole talk.

visual.title:
I wanted a skill
I could use on anybody.
visual.sub: Everyone has a return. Everyone has books. I came for the practical part — I stayed for the puzzle.

beats.opener: So — why accounting. I'll give you the real reason, and it's less romantic than it sounds.
beats.rest:
I wanted a skill I could use on anybody.

Biomedical engineering, I can help you if you're building a device. Salesforce, I can help you if you run Salesforce. Both of those come with conditions attached — you have to already be a certain kind of person before I'm any use to you.

Everybody files a return. Every business has books. So I went for the most practical version of that I could find.

beats.opener: And then I started studying for the CPA exams, and something happened that I didn't plan on.
beats.rest:
I got curious.

Not about the rules — about the shape of them. Why is it written this way. What was somebody trying to prevent when they drafted this. Who got burned before this existed.

I came for the practical part. I stayed because it turned out to be the most interesting rule system I've ever taken apart.
beats.marks: PAUSE two full beats before "I got curious" — longer than comfortable. RATE: say the cert list fast, say "I got curious" slow. The change IS the emphasis.

visual.title: So I went and got it.

items.sub: My third bachelor's degree.

items.lead: Enrolled Agent — admitted to practice before the IRS
items.sub: Business returns through Form 1120. Trial balance to Schedule L, book-to-tax on the M-1.
Completing the experience requirement.

visual.callout: Nobody needs a CISSP to reconcile a bank account. I sat for it anyway.

beats.opener: So I went and got the rulebook.
beats.rest:
Bachelor's in accounting from WGU, 2024. Enrolled Agent — admitted to practice before the IRS. I prepare business returns up through Form 1120, which means I read small-business books for a living. Trial balance to Schedule L, book-to-tax on the M-1. Books to returns is my normal commute.

And all four CPA exams passed. I'm finishing the experience requirement now.

beats.opener: Full disclosure on this slide, though. That accounting degree is my third bachelor's.
beats.rest:
And I passed the CISSP exam — which, same as the CPA, I don't get to put after my name until somebody endorses the experience.

So I'm currently sitting on two exams and two waiting rooms.

Nobody needs a CISSP to reconcile a bank account. I sat for it anyway.
beats.marks: SECOND LAUGH. Deadpan. No smile until after they react. Never say "I love learning" — the slide makes the point for you.

visual.title:
Now I'm the one
asking to see it.
visual.sub: Sales & use tax auditor, State of California — capital purchases · use tax · audit procedure.

beats.opener: Which brings me to now. I'm a sales and use tax auditor for the State of California.
beats.rest: The work is what it sounds like. I go into a business, I pull their records, and I test them. Capital equipment purchases are a standing part of what I test. So is use tax — which is the tax almost nobody self-reports correctly.

beats.opener: Here's the part I didn't expect about this job.
beats.rest:
I spent about a decade building the systems that produce these records. So now I open somebody's QuickBooks, or their ERP, and I can usually tell how an entry got made. Who made it. What screen they were looking at. Whether anyone ever looked at it again.

I know what it looks like from the inside, because I used to build the inside.
beats.marks: PAUSE — do not rush this. The section has walked ten minutes to get here. This is the payoff of slide 2: "none of this is accounting" — turns out all of it was.

visual.title:
I sing.
I play guitar.
visual.sub: Sometimes both at the same time.

beats.opener: Last thing before I get into the topics. Outside of work I sing, and I play guitar. Sometimes both at the same time.
beats.rest:
And there's a reason I didn't skip this slide. Music is the only other thing I do where the constraints are the entire point. There's a key. There's a time signature. Nobody has ever written a better song by deciding those didn't apply to them. The structure isn't in the way of the interesting part — the structure is what makes the interesting part possible.

That's more or less how I feel about accounting rules. Which I recognize is a strange sentence to say out loud.

So let's talk about one.
beats.marks: PAUSE before "So let's talk about one." That's the transition into Topic 1 — no dead air after it.

visual.title: Capitalize, or expense?

items.sub: What the rule actually asked for
My own contribution, specifically
The result, and whether it held
Lessons — said honestly

visual.callout: Two calls. One from the audit chair. One from the other chair.

beats.opener: Topic one. Capitalize, or expense.
beats.rest:
I'm going to walk you through two calls I've made. For each one I'll give you the same four things: what the requirement actually was, what I personally did about it, how it came out, and what I'd do differently.

The first call I made from the audit chair. Somebody else's books, and I was the one asking the questions.

The second one I made from the other chair.

Same question, both times. They did not feel remotely the same.
beats.marks: "The other chair" stays vague. Do not clarify, do not gesture, do not smile knowingly. You're planting something you won't pay off for ten minutes.

visual.title: I've made this call from three seats.

items.sub: Business returns through the 1120 — depreciation schedules, Form 4562, Section 179 and bonus elections, and book-to-tax depreciation on the M-1.
Every field exam tests whether capital purchases were identified correctly. That isn't adjacent to this decision — it is this decision, graded after the fact.
My own implementation costs, under ASC 350-40. That one is Example 2.

visual.callout: What I haven't done is post the month-end entry and run the rollforward. That's the part that's new — and it's the smallest part.

beats.cue: Three seats — name the gap first
beats.opener: Before the two examples, let me tell you where I've made this call before — because it probably isn't where you'd guess.
beats.rest:
I have not maintained a fixed asset subledger. I'd rather say that now than have it sitting under the next twenty minutes.

What I have done is make the capitalize-or-expense determination from three different seats.

On the return. I prepare business returns up through the 1120, which means depreciation schedules, Form 4562, Section 179 and bonus elections, and reconciling book depreciation to tax depreciation on the M-1. That reconciliation is the fixed asset question, restated in a different vocabulary.

In the audit. Every field exam I run tests whether capital purchases got identified correctly in the first place. That isn't adjacent to this decision — it is this decision, graded after the fact, by me.

And in the build, where the cost was my own. That's the second example.
beats.marks: Even and unhurried. You are sizing a gap, not confessing to one. Same energy as "none of this is accounting."

beats.opener: So here's the honest shape of it.
beats.rest:
I know the rule. I've applied it, and I've tested other people's application of it — which is a harder version of the same skill, because I have to defend my answer to someone who disagrees.

What's new is the posting and the rollforward. That's a week, not a quarter.

And I'd much rather you know exactly which part is new than find out in March.
beats.marks: Then MOVE. Do not pause for reassurance — going straight into Example 1 is what makes it read as sized rather than apologized for.

visual.title:
It was filed
under repairs.
visual.sub: A field audit at CDTFA. Details disguised — no names, nothing identifying.

beats.opener: The first call I made from the audit chair. Let me take you inside a real one.
beats.rest:
This is from my CDTFA work, so the details are disguised — no names, nothing identifying. But the decision is real, and it's one I make regularly.

And I want to start with what most people get wrong about a sales tax audit. Everyone assumes we only look at sales. We don't. Every field audit examines what the business bought, too.
beats.marks: Plain and unhurried. You are inviting them somewhere, not performing.

visual.kick: The requirement · where a purchase exam looks
visual.title:
Two piles. Only one of them
is any work.

a.lines:
A list of things
somebody already
decided were assets

b.lines:
Repairs, supplies,
consumables — and
whatever got misfiled

visual.tail: The schedule is the easy pile. The expense accounts are where you earn the day.

beats.opener: A purchase exam starts by splitting what the business bought into two piles: fixed asset additions, and expense accounts.
beats.rest:
The fixed asset schedule is the easy pile. It's a list of things somebody already decided were assets, and it's the first place any auditor looks — a taxable equipment purchase sitting on the depreciation schedule is not hiding from anybody.

The expense accounts are where you actually earn the day. And of those, repairs and maintenance is where I spend my time — because that is where assets go to hide.

Not from tax. From detection.
beats.marks: "Not from tax. From detection." — this correction is doing real work. Say it as a clarification, not a punchline.

visual.title: In repairs and maintenance:

items.sub: Line-by-line through the account, which is most of the job.
So nothing was collected at the register — which makes it a use tax question.

items.lead: Equipment, freight, and installation on one invoice
items.sub: A spray booth for an auto body shop.
Which is exactly why it had never been looked at.

beats.opener: So I'm going through repairs and maintenance line by line, which is most of the job, and there it is.
beats.rest:
About twenty thousand dollars. Out-of-state vendor, so no tax was collected at the point of sale. Equipment, freight, and installation, all on one invoice — a spray booth.

Coded to repairs. And nowhere on the depreciation schedule.
beats.marks: Let the last line sit. Do not explain it yet — the next two slides are the explanation.

visual.title:
Two rules. One invoice.
Two different numbers.

a.lines:
Purchase price.
Separately stated
installation labor is
excluded — Reg 1546.

b.lines:
Price plus freight
plus installation —
everything to get it
in place and working.

visual.tail: The two rules are asking different questions, so they don't produce the same number.

beats.opener: And here is the part I find genuinely interesting, because this one invoice gets measured twice, two different ways.
beats.rest:
For my purposes — the use tax measure — the starting point is the purchase price. But separately stated charges for installation labor are excluded from the measure of tax under Regulation 1546, and separately stated delivery to the purchaser generally is too.

For their books, under ASC 360, it's the opposite instruction. Freight and installation go into the asset's basis, because basis is everything required to get it in place and working.

Same invoice. Two different numbers. Not because anyone is wrong — because the two rules are answering different questions. Mine is asking what was purchased for use in California. Theirs is asking what the asset cost.
beats.marks: This is your credibility slide with the technical interviewer. Unhurried, and do not apologize for the detail.

visual.kick: The call I make — and the one I don't
visual.title: Use tax never depended on the pile.

items.lead: The tax was due either way
items.sub: Tangible personal property, bought out of state, used in California, no tax paid to the vendor. Which account it sat in changes nothing about that.

items.lead: But it was misclassified, and I said so
items.sub: Added capability rather than restoring it, useful life in years, expensed to R&M and missing from the schedule for three years. That's a books problem, not a tax problem — and not my assessment to make.

items.lead: And the misclassification is why nobody had caught it
items.sub: Additions on the depreciation schedule get reviewed. Costs buried in R&M don't. The coding didn't create the liability. It hid it.

visual.callout: Which is the actual reason this story belongs in a capitalization presentation.

beats.cue: The honest scope of my call
beats.opener: Now — I want to be precise about what I actually decided, because it's narrower than you might expect.
beats.rest: The use tax did not depend on the classification at all. Tangible personal property, purchased out of state, used in California, no tax paid to the vendor. Use tax is due. Whether they called it a repair or an asset changes nothing about that conclusion, and I want to say that plainly because it would be easy to overclaim here.

beats.cue: The part that wasn't my job
beats.opener: But the classification was wrong, and I raised it anyway — because it wasn't my assessment, it was their books.
beats.rest:
It added capability rather than restoring it. Its useful life is measured in years. It was expensed to repairs and missing from the depreciation schedule for three years running.

So their own two records disagreed with each other. Their own records told on them.
beats.marks: PAUSE after "told on them." Add nothing to it.

beats.opener: And here's why the pile mattered, even though the tax didn't turn on it.
beats.rest:
It's the reason nobody had ever caught it. Additions on the depreciation schedule get reviewed — by their CPA, by their lender, by me. Costs buried in repairs and maintenance don't get reviewed by anyone.

The misclassification didn't create the liability. It hid it, for three years.

Which is the actual reason this story belongs in a capitalization presentation.
beats.marks: This is the beat that answers "why does an auditor care about capitalization." Land it deliberately.

visual.title:
It has to cut
both ways.
visual.sub: The genuine repairs in that same account — compressor service, filter changes — I left alone.

beats.opener: One more thing about that account, and this is the part I'd want you to hold me to.
beats.rest:
That same account had real repairs in it. Compressor service. Filter changes. I left every one of them alone.

Because if the call only ever goes one direction, it isn't judgment — it's a shakedown. A position I can defend is one that would have gone the other way if the facts had.
beats.marks: Say "shakedown" evenly. No edge on it. The restraint is the point.

visual.kick: How it came out · what I'd change
visual.title: It held. And nobody was cheating.

items.lead: The assessment held at the exit conference
items.sub: Walked the owner and their CPA through both pieces — what they owed, and separately, what their books had wrong.
The invoice sounded like a repair vendor, so it went where repair invoices go, and sat there for three years.

items.lead: The call got made at data entry
items.sub: By default, by the person with the least context, with no threshold to check against.

visual.callout: Which is the lesson: that decision belongs at the point of entry, on purpose, under a written policy. Hold that thought.

beats.opener: At the exit conference I walked the owner and their CPA through both pieces — what they owed me, and separately, what their books had wrong. The assessment held.
beats.rest:
And here's what I actually took away from it, which isn't about tax at all.

Nobody was cheating. The invoice sounded like a repair vendor, so it got filed where repair invoices go, and it sat there wrong for three years. Nobody ever revisited it.

That classification was made at data entry, by default, by the person with the least context, with no threshold to check against.

beats.cue: What I'd change — point of entry
beats.opener: So what would I change? Not the audit. The moment the decision happened.
beats.rest:
That call belongs at the point of entry — on purpose, under a written policy, by someone who knows what the threshold is.

Hold onto that. I'm going to build it in Topic 2.
beats.marks: PLANT for Topic 2, build 3. Say it lightly — do not oversell the setup.

visual.title:
The other chair
was mine.
visual.sub: Four months of my own time, on a system I built. No consultant invoice — the invoice was me.

beats.opener: The second call. Same question — capitalize, or expense. And this time the cost was mine.
beats.rest:
The other chair was mine.

Remember PMify and Survey Builder, the two things I built on Salesforce at ForensisGroup. That was roughly four months of development. There was no consultant invoice for any of it.

The invoice was me.
beats.marks: PAYOFF of the plant on the Topic 1 title card. Let "the invoice was me" sit before you move.

visual.title:
A subscription is never an asset.
The setup might be.
visual.tail: And internal payroll counts. "We didn't pay a vendor" is not an answer.

beats.opener: So what does the rule actually require? This is ASC 350-40 — cloud computing arrangements, as amended by ASU 2018-15.
beats.rest:
The subscription fee itself is never an asset. That's rent, you expense it as you consume it.

But implementation costs split. Configuration, customization, coding and testing can be capitalized. Training and data conversion are expensed regardless of when they happen.

And the part that made this my problem: internal payroll counts. "We didn't pay an outside vendor" is not an answer. My four months was a real cost, and the question of whether some of it belonged on the balance sheet was a real question.

visual.title:
Nothing. Nobody asked —
including me.
visual.sub: It ran through payroll and was expensed as incurred. There was no capitalization discussion at the time.

beats.opener: I'm not going to dress this up. What I did at the time was nothing.
beats.rest:
It ran through payroll and got expensed as incurred. There was no capitalization analysis, no memo, no discussion. Nobody asked.

Including me. And I was the one who knew both halves of it.
beats.marks: Do not soften this and do not rush past it. The credibility of everything after depends on saying it flat.

visual.title: I've since worked it like an auditor.

items.sub: So any capitalizable number now would be a reconstruction, not a measurement.

items.lead: The mix was scoping and training heavy
items.sub: Both of which are expensed under the standard anyway.
It would not have moved a reader's understanding of the statements.

visual.callout: Expense was the right answer. But I reached it the wrong way — and a defensible answer without documentation is still an undocumented answer.

beats.opener: So I went back and worked it the way I'd work someone else's file.
beats.rest:
There were no contemporaneous time records, which means any number I produce now is a reconstruction, not a measurement. The mix was heavily scoping and training, both of which get expensed anyway. And at that scale it was immaterial — it wouldn't have changed how anyone read the statements.

So expense was the right answer.

beats.opener: But I got to the right answer the wrong way.
beats.rest:
I didn't conclude expense. I defaulted to expense, and then got lucky that the default happened to be correct.

A defensible answer without documentation is still an undocumented answer.
beats.marks: SLOW. This is the line the whole example exists for.

visual.title: Three things, and I'd do them on day one.

items.lead: Track the hours while it's happening
items.sub: Not to force capitalization — to preserve the option. Once the quarter closes, the ability to measure is gone.

items.lead: Write the memo even when the answer is "expense"
items.sub: An hour of work turns a default into a position.

items.lead: Know when scale flips the answer
items.sub: Same framework, different outcome — your NetSuite and Ramp implementations lived this exact question.

visual.callout: And the twist people miss: a capitalized cloud implementation cost isn't a fixed asset. It's a prepaid-type asset amortizing into the same operating line as the subscription. Never depreciation.

beats.opener: Three things I'd do differently, and none of them are hard.
beats.rest:
Track the hours while it's happening — not to force capitalization, but to preserve the option, because once the quarter closes the ability to measure it is gone for good.

Write the memo even when the answer is expense. An hour of work turns a default into a position.

And know when scale flips the answer. Same framework, different outcome — and I'd guess your NetSuite and Ramp implementations lived this exact question at a size where it mattered.

beats.opener: And one technical thing that catches people, since we're on it.
beats.rest:
A capitalized cloud implementation cost isn't a fixed asset. It doesn't go to PP&E and it never gets depreciated. It's a prepaid-type asset that amortizes into the same operating expense line as the subscription itself.

So it's a capitalization question that never produces a fixed asset.
beats.marks: Deliver as a genuine aside, not a flex. If it reads as showing off it costs you.

visual.title:
Both calls got made
by whoever was closest.
visual.sub: One by a bookkeeper with no rule. One by me, with every rule — and still no memo.

beats.opener: Two calls, two chairs, and the same failure underneath both of them.
beats.rest:
In the first one, a bookkeeper made a capitalization decision by default, because nobody had given them a threshold to check against.

In the second one, I made a capitalization decision by default — and I knew the standard. I just didn't write anything down.

Both calls got made by whoever happened to be closest to the transaction, with nothing to follow.

beats.cue: What the two examples were for
beats.opener: And that's why I picked those two.
beats.rest:
Not because they were the biggest numbers I've touched. Because one of them I caught, and one of them I missed — and I'd rather show you both than show you two wins.

The judgment is the part that transfers. The posting is the part I learn.
beats.marks: This is the sentence that answers the bookkeeping question without ever restating it.

beats.opener: Which is the pattern I told you I'd come back to.
beats.rest:
I did the job by hand. I felt exactly where it hurt.

So let me tell you what I'd build.
beats.marks: THROUGH-LINE pass 2 of 3. This is the hinge into Topic 2 — do not pause after "what I'd build."

visual.title:
The first
ninety days.
visual.sub: Learn the job honestly. Contribute like a builder.

beats.opener: Topic two. My first ninety days.
beats.rest: This is a learning plan and a contribution plan at the same time, and I want to be straight with you about which parts are which.

visual.title:
I haven't done
international accounting.
visual.sub: I understand the concepts in theory. I just don't have the reps — yet.

beats.opener: So let me say the obvious part out loud, because you already know it. I haven't done international accounting.
beats.rest:
What I do have is the standards. FAR tested consolidation and currency translation — ASC 830, intercompany eliminations, the CTA running through OCI instead of income. I understand the concepts in theory.

What I don't have is the reps.
beats.marks: PAUSE. Full stop. Do not rush to reassure them — the silence is the confidence.

beats.cue: But you've watched me do this
beats.opener: But you've just watched me do this four times.
beats.rest:
I hadn't done data architecture, and I wrote the VBA and moved it into a real database. I hadn't done Salesforce, and six months later I was the department. I hadn't done accounting at all, and I went and got a third bachelor's degree and passed four CPA exams.

I don't wait until I'm qualified. I go get qualified, and I do it while the work is happening.

So here's the ninety days.
beats.marks: This is the whole intro cashing in. Confident, not defensive. You're stating a record, not arguing.

visual.title: Four problems, and I know their names.

items.sub: JPY and EUR into USD — and the CTA runs through OCI, not the income statement.
Intercompany, investment, minority interest — in OneWorld or by hand.
Arm's-length documentation that survives Section 482 and a foreign authority's review.

items.lead: Indirect tax — VAT and Consumption Tax
items.sub: Which is the discipline I already run daily on California sales and use tax.

beats.opener: The terrain has four problems in it, and I already know their names.
beats.rest:
Currency translation under ASC 830 — Japan's yen and France's euro into dollars, with the translation adjustment running through OCI rather than income. Consolidation and eliminations — intercompany, investment, minority interest. Transfer pricing — documentation that has to survive both Section 482 and a foreign authority looking at the same transaction from the other side.

And indirect tax. VAT and Japanese Consumption Tax. Which is the one I'd argue I already do — that is the same discipline as California sales and use tax, and I run it every day.
beats.marks: Say the fourth one with a little more weight. It's the one place you're already an expert.

visual.title: Do the job by hand.

items.sub: Follow Japan's reporting package through translation and eliminations into the consolidated statements. Once, by hand.

items.lead: Sit with whoever does it now
items.sub: Not to review it. To learn it from the person who actually knows where it breaks.
Entities, currencies, elimination rules — what the system does versus what a human does after it.

beats.opener: Month one: do the job by hand.
beats.rest:
I want to follow one close all the way through manually. Take Japan's reporting package, walk it through translation and eliminations, and land it in the consolidated statements — once, by hand, slowly.

Not because that's efficient. Because that's the only way I've ever actually learned anything. And I want to sit with whoever does it today, not to review their work, but to find out where it breaks.

And I'll map how OneWorld is configured — what the system does automatically, versus what a person quietly fixes afterward.
beats.marks: You are deliberately echoing slide 7. Do not point at it — they'll feel it.

visual.title: Feel where it hurts.

items.lead: Own real close tasks, under review
items.sub: Reconciliations and translation entries that are mine — checked by someone senior until they don't need to be.
Where do the hours actually go? Nobody knows, because nobody has ever written it down.

items.lead: Pick one automation with the controller
items.sub: Highest pain, lowest risk. Their call, not mine.

beats.opener: Month two: feel where it hurts.
beats.rest:
By now I should be carrying real close tasks — reconciliations, translation entries — mine, under review by someone senior until that review stops being necessary.

And while I'm in there, I'm timing it. Where do the hours actually go? Most teams can't answer that, not because they're careless, but because nobody has ever had a reason to write it down.

Then I pick one automation with the controller. Highest pain, lowest risk. That's their call, not mine — I'm new.

visual.title: Build the thing that removes it.

items.lead: My slice of the close, fully owned
items.sub: No training wheels.
With a before-and-after number attached to it.

items.lead: Both documented well enough to survive me
items.sub: If it only works while I'm in the room, I haven't finished.

beats.opener: Month three: build the thing that removes it.
beats.rest:
My slice of the close is fully mine by then, no training wheels. The first automation is live, with a before-and-after number attached — not a claim, a measurement.

And both are documented well enough to survive me. If it only works while I'm in the room, I haven't actually finished it.

visual.title: You've seen this plan before.
visual.tail: It isn't a plan I wrote for this interview. It's the only way I've ever worked.

beats.opener: And I want to point at something, because I promised I would.
beats.rest:
This is the same plan I've run my entire career. I did the bench work, then I built the lab system. I did the data entry, then I built the database.

So: I do your close by hand, I find out exactly where it hurts, and then I build the thing that takes it away.

That isn't a plan I wrote for this interview. It's just the only way I've ever worked.
beats.marks: THROUGH-LINE pass 3 of 3 — the payoff of slide 7. Slow, and let the third row of the diagram sit before you speak over it.

visual.title:
Instrument
the close.
visual.sub: Treat books-to-reports like a pipeline: measure where the hours go, then remove one manual step every month.

beats.opener: Which brings me to the one idea I was asked to bring. Instrument the close.
beats.rest:
Treat books-to-reports like a pipeline. Measure where the hours actually go, then remove exactly one manual step every month — small builds, each one shipped with a before-and-after number.

Most closes never get faster. Not because anyone is bad at their job, but because nobody owns the word "faster." Everyone owns their piece, and their piece works.

I'm offering to own faster.
beats.marks: PAUSE before "I'm offering to own faster." That's the sentence you want them repeating later.

visual.title: And I'd start with these.

items.sub: Instrument it before touching it. You cannot remove a step you haven't measured — and this needs no domain expertise, so I can build it in month one.
Automated completeness and tie-out checks on subsidiary packages, run before a human ever opens them.
Remember the spray booth. Cleaner books upstream is a faster close downstream.

visual.callout: Measure it, stop the rework, then stop the error. In that order.

beats.opener: Three builds, in a deliberate order.
beats.rest:
First, the close clock — instrument it before I touch anything. You can't remove a step you haven't measured, and this one needs no international accounting knowledge at all, which is exactly why it's first. I can build it while I'm still learning.

Second, a package pre-check. Automated completeness and tie-out checks on the subsidiary packages, run before a human ever opens them. Stop the rework.

Third — and this is the one I planted twenty minutes ago — point-of-entry classification rules.

visual.title: A rules layer in front of NetSuite.
visual.tail: Remember the spray booth. This is the thing that would have caught it on day one.

beats.opener: This is the spray booth, solved at the front instead of found at the back.
beats.rest:
A transaction hits Ramp. Rules and categorization run on it immediately. Routine and below threshold, it auto-codes as an expense. Above threshold, it routes to a short capex review queue instead of being coded by whoever is closest. A cloud or SaaS vendor gets flagged for the capitalize-versus-expense split we just talked about.

Then the approved coding syncs to NetSuite.

The flag happens the moment the invoice lands — not three weeks later at close, and not three years later with me sitting across the table.
beats.marks: The last clause is the callback. Say it dry — it's funnier and sharper if you don't lean on it.

visual.title:
And when the auditors
get bigger.
visual.sub: I'd go get the Certified Internal Auditor — so I'm already that person before the audit shows up, not during it.

beats.opener: One thing beyond ninety days, because Vast is going to keep scaling and the audit gets bigger with it.
beats.rest:
At some point the external audit stops being a formality. Somebody on the inside has to already speak that language — to know what they're going to ask for before they ask, and to have it ready.

I'd go get the Certified Internal Auditor for that. Not because the role requires it. Because I'd rather be that person before the audit shows up than during it.

And I want to be honest about the timeline — that's three parts and about a year. It is not a ninety-day promise.
beats.marks: The honesty about the timeline is doing real work here. Do not skip it to sound more impressive.

visual.title: So — in ninety days.

items.sub: Not shadowed. Owned.
Measured, not claimed.

items.lead: And a close that gets a step faster every month after that
items.sub: Because somebody finally owns faster.

beats.opener: So, in ninety days: my close tasks owned — not shadowed, owned.
beats.rest:
One automation live, with a real number attached to it.

And a close that gets a step faster every month after that, because somebody finally owns faster.

I was the guy
entering the data.

beats.opener: I started by telling you I was the guy entering the data.
beats.rest:
Every job since, I did the work by hand first, found out where it hurt, and then built the thing that took it away. The lab system. The database. The payment sync. The audit chair.

I'd like to do that here.
beats.marks: Full circle to slide 3. Land it, then STOP. Do not add a summary sentence — let the silence be the ending.
